1 Motivation (p.1)
The Cedar pilot studies water use in a greenhouse. The purpose is to compare a timer schedule with
a moisture-sensor schedule. Both schedules were tested for fourteen days under the same
greenhouse conditions. The pilot measures water volume and plant height. It does not investigate
outdoor farms or long-term crop yields. Each schedule used six trays with the same soil and
seedlings. The team recorded irrigation volume daily and measured plant height at the end. The
report is a small descriptive pilot rather than a claim about all crops. The practical motivation is
reducing unnecessary irrigation while maintaining growth. The same caretaker inspected both
groups each morning. Equipment failures were recorded before daily totals were calculated.

2 Timer Results (p.2)
The timer schedule delivered 42 liters of water across its six trays during the fourteen-day pilot.
Mean final plant height was 18 centimeters. The timer ran at fixed intervals independent of soil
moisture. Daily records showed that some irrigation occurred while the soil was already moist. No
timer failures were reported during the observation period. These measurements describe the timer
group only. Water volume includes all irrigation during the pilot and is not a per-tray quantity. Height
is a group mean measured at the end. The report does not provide variance estimates or a
significance test. Future tests should include different soils, larger groups and longer observation
periods.

3 Sensor Results (p.3)
The sensor schedule delivered 30 liters of water across its six trays during the fourteen-day pilot.
Mean final plant height was 19 centimeters. The sensor activated irrigation when measured moisture
fell below the configured threshold. One loose cable was repaired before the first day of
measurement. No failures occurred during the recorded period. The pilot therefore observed lower
total water volume with the sensor schedule, alongside a similar final plant height. The report does
not establish causality or long-term crop yield. The conclusion recommends a larger controlled trial
before changing greenhouse practice. Threshold calibration and sensor maintenance require further
study. The authors explicitly limit these observations to the tested trays and conditions.
